questions.stem: What is the key difference between xylem and phloem transport?

options.text: Xylem transports water and minerals upward; phloem transports sugars up and down
Xylem uses active transport; phloem does not
Xylem transports sugars; phloem transports water

questions.explanation: Xylem transports water and minerals in one direction (upward from roots to leaves), while phloem transports dissolved sugars in both directions between sources and sinks.

questions.stem: Which transport tissue consists of dead cells?
questions.explanation: Xylem vessels are made of dead cells with no cytoplasm, forming hollow tubes reinforced with lignin. Phloem sieve tubes are living cells (though they lack nuclei).

questions.stem: What drives the movement of water through xylem?

options.text: The pumping action of the heart
Transpiration pull, cohesion between water molecules, and root pressure

questions.explanation: Water moves through xylem driven by the transpiration pull (evaporation from leaves creates tension), cohesion between water molecules, and root pressure from osmosis in the roots.

questions.stem: Why does phloem transport require energy but xylem transport does not?

options.text: Phloem loads sugars by active transport using ATP from companion cells; xylem is driven passively by transpiration

questions.explanation: Phloem transport requires energy because sucrose is actively loaded into sieve tubes by companion cells. Xylem transport is passive, driven by the evaporation of water from leaves.

questions.stem: What is the advantage of the double circulatory system in mammals compared to fish?

options.text: Blood passes through the heart twice, maintaining higher pressure for efficient oxygen delivery to tissues
It only requires two heart chambers

questions.explanation: In a double system, blood is re-pressurised by the heart after passing through the lungs, so it reaches body tissues at a higher pressure than in the single system of fish, enabling more efficient delivery.

questions.stem: How are arteries, veins, and capillaries structurally different?

options.text: They are all identical in structure
Arteries have thick elastic walls; veins have thinner walls with valves; capillaries have walls one cell thick

questions.explanation: Arteries have thick muscular and elastic walls to withstand high pressure. Veins have thinner walls with valves to prevent backflow. Capillaries have walls one cell thick for efficient substance exchange.

questions.stem: In both animals and plants, why are transport systems essential?

options.text: Large organisms have a small surface area to volume ratio, making diffusion alone too slow to supply all cells
They are needed for reproduction only
They are only needed for movement

questions.explanation: Large multicellular organisms have a small surface area to volume ratio, meaning diffusion alone cannot supply all cells quickly enough. Transport systems deliver substances efficiently throughout the organism.
